The AOR on the same row, 1.36 (0.98 to 1.89) p = .07, is fully self-consistent (see ame_row_aor_control), which localises the error to the printed AME interval rather than to the fitted model: a single mis-set digit in the upper bound would reconcile the row. findings.notes: Produced by check_estimate_ci (CLI: check-ci). Nine of 50 odds ratios have a p recovered from their own CI differing from the printed p, in every case by less than 0.016 -- under one unit in the second decimal at which these p-values are printed. Three considerations argue for benign rounding rather than an integrity problem, and the editorial stage should weight them. (a) The direction is MIXED (4 up, 5 down); a paper shifting p-values toward significance would show a one-directional pattern. (b) Recovery uses a normal approximation, whereas the paper used SAS PROC SURVEY on a stratified multistage CLUSTER sample, where Wald intervals use a t-multiplier on design degrees of freedom rather than 1.96 -- that alone displaces recovered p at this magnitude. (c) The CI bounds are printed to only 2 decimals, so the recovered SE carries visible quantisation. Two of the nine (AOR 1.61 p=.04 and AOR 0.49 p=.04) carry paper claims and sit adjacent to the .05 threshold, so they deserve naming; neither crosses it under either reading. Recorded at the tool's severity for completeness, with the caveat that this cluster most likely reflects reporting precision.

findings.title: Aor ci consistency bulk (Table 2 (30 AORs) and Table 3 (20 AORs), all non-reference rows)
findings.description: Produced by check_estimate_ci (CLI: check-ci), run on all 50 estimates. Every odds ratio sits at the LOG-scale midpoint of its own interval -- the correct symmetry test for a ratio measure, and the one that misfires on roughly a third of ratio estimates if done on the linear scale. Not one fails it. All four AORs the paper leads with reconcile exactly with both interval and printed p: 1.71 (1.17-2.49) p=.006 recovers 0.0054; 0.57 (0.34-0.95) p=.03 recovers 0.0320; 0.46 (0.24-0.88) p=.02 recovers 0.0191; 0.31 (0.14-0.66) p=.002 recovers 0.0031. This is the largest single block of checking in the sweep and it is overwhelmingly clean; the denominator matters when reading the nine flags above.

findings.notes: The Key Points and abstract state two directional conclusions without qualification, but the underlying comparisons are mostly null. For the protective claim among people WITH disability, 2 of 9 veteran-vs-nonveteran contrasts in Table 2 are significant (planning at 1 limitation, attempt at 2 limitations); the other 7 are null, and NONE of the three contrasts at >=3 limitations -- the most disabled group -- reaches significance. The two significant results also fall at different disability levels for different outcomes, with no consistent gradient. For the elevated-risk claim among people WITHOUT disability, 1 of 3 contrasts is significant (planning, AOR 1.71), while ideation (1.12) and attempt (0.98) are flat. Every significant estimate does point in the claimed direction, so this is over-generalisation of scope rather than misstatement of direction, and the tables themselves report the numbers correctly. Flagged because the Key Points is the most widely read and least qualified part of a JAMA Network Open paper.

findings.title: Headline claim failed own sensitivity analysis
findings.description: The Key Points assert that military service was associated with higher suicide risk among people WITHOUT disability. Within Table 2 that claim rests on a single contrast, AOR 1.71 for planning -- and the authors report, in the very sentence introducing it, that it did NOT retain significance in their multiple-imputation sensitivity analysis. The corresponding Table 3 subgroup result (AOR 1.61, p = .04) did retain significance, so the claim is not unsupported; but a headline conclusion whose primary supporting estimate fails the paper's own robustness check, with that failure disclosed only in body text and absent from the Key Points, is a reporting asymmetry worth surfacing. Credit where due

findings.notes: The sensitivity analysis runs on N = 241 675, the full adult sample, versus 231 099 in the main analysis -- 10 576 records restored by imputation. Per the flow diagram this necessarily includes imputing the OUTCOME (suicide ideation/planning/attempt) for 1 141 respondents and the EXPOSURE (disability status) for 2 044, alongside 7 261 with missing covariates. Imputing the dependent variable is generally discouraged (it adds no information about the outcome-predictor association while propagating the imputation model's assumptions into the estimate), and imputing the exposure compounds it. This matters more than usual because claims turn on disagreements between the two analyses in both directions -- one headline result loses significance under imputation, another gains it. Marked indeterminate rather than suspicious: the imputation model is not described in the available text and eTables 3-4 were inaccessible, so the magnitude cannot be established. Flagged for human review of Supplement 1.

findings.title: Table1 weighted n rounding blocks
findings.description: These three blocks miss the total by exactly one unit (-1, +1, -1). At the tool's default tolerance of 0.5 they register as discrepancies, which is why they are recorded explicitly. They are not anomalies: these are survey-weighted population estimates, each independently rounded to a whole person before printing, so a k-category block can drift by up to k/2. Re-run with the tolerance appropriate to that rounding (2.5, 2.0, 1.5) all three pass. Recorded so the +/-1 residuals are on the record and cannot later be mistaken for a suppressed finding -- the correct reading is that all ten blocks of Table 1 reconcile.

findings.title: Threshold p recovery (Table 2, all rows printed as P < .001 (12 of 30 AORs))

findings.title: Grim family inapplicable (Whole paper -- Table 1 percentages, Tables 2-3 odds ratios)
findings.description: Recording a deliberate non-application, because running these tools here is the likeliest route to a false accusation on this paper. GRIM, GRIMMER, SPRITE and DEBIT all require observations that are integers over an integer denominator. Every percentage in Table 1 is survey-weighted: its denominator is a sum of sampling weights, not a count of people, so a weighted percentage is not of the form k/n and GRIM-family granularity arguments do not hold -- applying them would manufacture impossibilities from entirely ordinary cells. The paper reports no means and no standard deviations at all, so GRIMMER and SPRITE have no input. reconstruct_2x2 was also declined: the unweighted cell counts needed

findings.title: Baseline similarity inapplicable
findings.description: Declined deliberately. Carlisle-Stouffer-Fisher and the Bayesian dispersion test detect groups MORE similar than randomisation permits; both presuppose random allocation, so that baseline p-values should be Uniform(0,1). Nothing was randomised here -- veteran status is a self-reported characteristic and the groups are expected to differ profoundly (91.0% vs 44.0% male, 48.8% vs 17.8% aged 65 or over). The observed pattern of uniformly LOW p-values is the substantive finding that motivated covariate adjustment, and the rulebook's red flag (uniformly HIGH p-values, tau-hat > 1) is not even definable in this design. Running either test would be a category error yielding a meaningless verdict. T

findings.title: No power analysis stated (Method, 'Statistical Analysis')
findings.description: No a-priori power or sample-size calculation is stated, so verify_power_analysis cannot run -- only alpha is given; effect size and target power are both absent. This is unremarkable for a secondary analysis of an existing national survey, where N is fixed by the data source. It is recorded because it bears on interpretation elsewhere: the paper's own limitations concede 'smaller cell sizes after stratifying sample groups to veteran and nonveterans', and the widest intervals in Table 2 (e.g. attempt at >=3 limitations, 0.32 to 1.45) fall precisely where veteran cell counts are thinnest. Precision within strata, not overall sample size, is the binding constraint on the null results.
